record.paper_title: Trimer Covers in the Triangular Grid: Twenty Mostly Open Problems
record.original_question: Let T103(a,b) denote the number of tilings of the (a,b)-benzel in which right stones are allowed, left stones are forbidden, and all three bone orientations are allowed. Is it true that T103(n, 2n-3) = (3n+3)(3n-7)!/((n-5)! (2n-1)!) for every n >= 5, with the same formula also yielding 0 for n = 3 and n = 4 if one formally interprets 1/(-1)! and 1/(-2)! as 0?

evidence.quote: For 0 <= i, j <= 1 and 0 <= k <= 3 we define Tijk (a, b) as the number of ways to tile the (a, b)-benzel if the set of allowed prototiles contains the right stone iff i = 1, contains the left stone iff j = 1, and contains k of the bones. We say that such a tiling is an i, j, k tiling.

Problem 6: Is is true that T103 (n, 2n - 3) = (3n + 3)(3n - 7)!/(n - 5)!(2n - 1)! for n >= 5? (The formula also works for n = 3 and n = 4 if one treats 1/(-1)! and 1/(-2)! as 0.) Equality has been verified for 5 <= n <= 16.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the triangular grid in the plane, viewed as the tiling of the plane by unit equilateral triangles in two orientations (upward- and downward-pointing). For positive integers a, b, the (a,b)-benzel is a specific finite, three-fold rotationally symmetric region in the triangular grid (built from upward and downward unit triangles, equivalently from hexagonal cells of the dual honeycomb), defined as follows: starting from the hexagonal cell tiling, one carves out the region whose boundary is determined by parameters a and b in the standard way that produces benzel-shaped regions (the boundary is determined by truncating an appropriate hexagon so that the region has 3-fold rotational symmetry).

The prototiles used to tile such regions are:
• Right(-pointing) stone: the union of three pairwise adjacent hexagonal cells whose centers form a small triangle pointing right.
• Left(-pointing) stone: the same shape but with the small triangle of centers pointing left.
• Three "bones": each bone is the union of three contiguous hexagonal cells whose centers are collinear (the three bones correspond to the three possible orientations: vertical, rising, and falling).

For i, j ∈ {0,1} and k ∈ {0,1,2,3}, let T_{ijk}(a,b) denote the number of tilings of the (a,b)-benzel by these prototiles in which right stones are allowed iff i=1, left stones are allowed iff j=1, and exactly k of the three bone orientations are allowed.

Prove or disprove: for every integer n ≥ 5,
T_{103}(n, 2n−3) = (3n+3) · (3n−7)! / ( (n−5)! · (2n−1)! ),
where T_{103} counts tilings in which right stones are permitted, left stones are forbidden, and all three bone orientations are permitted. (With the convention that 1/(−1)! and 1/(−2)! are interpreted as 0, the same formula yields 0 for n = 3 and n = 4.)
artifact.status_search_result: Propp's benzel tilings status page lists Problem 6 of the twenty problems as Open. No published resolution of the conjectured closed form for T_{103}(n, 2n−3) was found in searches of related arXiv work (Kim–Propp pentagonal number theorem; generalized compression; abacus bijection; Lai's nearly symmetric hexagons).
